title: Mechatronics
full_title: Mechatronics: Sensors, Actuators and Embedded Control
tagline: Sensors, signal conditioning and data acquisition, microcontrollers, electric motors and drives, hydraulic and pneumatic actuators, and motion control
summary: Mechatronics combines mechanisms, electronics and software into machines that sense and act. The course covers sensors, signal conditioning and data acquisition, microcontrollers and real-time software, DC, stepper and brushless motors and their drives, hydraulic and pneumatic actuation, and closed-loop motion control, ending with the design of complete mechatronic systems.
overview: Mechatronics is the design of machines in which mechanisms, electronics and software work together: sensors measure the state of a mechanical process, a digital controller decides what to do, and power electronics drive actuators that act on the process. The inkjet printer, the anti-lock brake, the robot arm, the CNC machine tool and the 3D printer are all mechatronic systems, and in each the precision and flexibility come less from the mechanism itself than from feedback — an imprecise mechanism inside a well-designed loop behaves as a precise one.

The course follows the signal path around such a loop. It starts with the elements of a mechatronic system and the circuit basics needed to connect them (dividers and loading, RC circuits, inductive loads and transistor switches), then covers sensors and their static and dynamic specifications, the conditioning of their signals (operational amplifiers, bridges, filters, noise) and their conversion to numbers (quantisation, sampling and aliasing). The microcontroller chapter deals with what happens inside the controller — number formats, timers and PWM, interrupts, real-time scheduling and the implementation of a digital PID controller.

The second half turns to actuation and control: DC, stepper and brushless motors with their models, drives and gearing; hydraulic and pneumatic actuators, including the orifice equation and the hydraulic natural frequency; and motion control of servo axes — trajectory generation, PD and PID control, feedforward, friction and mechanical resonance. The final chapter treats the system as a whole: requirements, error, power and thermal budgets, electromagnetic compatibility, reliability, functional safety, and case studies.

The course assumes the control-systems course (transfer functions, time and frequency response, PID control) and basic mechanics. Its difficulty lies in the interfaces between domains: most failures of real mechatronic systems come from an interaction that no single-domain analysis shows — a ground loop, an aliased PWM ripple, a resonance inside the loop, a safety function left to ordinary software. Each chapter therefore works quantitative examples across those boundaries, and the exercises ask for numbers as well as for design judgement.
outcomes: Identify the sensors, signal conditioning, controller, drivers, actuators and process of a mechatronic system, and draw up its error, timing and power budgets.
Calculate loading errors, RC time constants and the switching transients of inductive loads, and specify protection for transistor drivers.
Select a sensor for a measurement from its static and dynamic specifications, including encoders, strain gauges, accelerometers and temperature sensors.
Design an amplifier, bridge and anti-aliasing filter chain for a sensor, and calculate its resolution, noise and alias frequencies.
Configure microcontroller timers and PWM, check the schedulability of periodic tasks, and implement a discrete PID controller with anti-windup.
Model DC, stepper and brushless motors, calculate torque–speed characteristics, time constants, gear ratios and rms torque, and size a motor and drive.
Calculate the forces, flows, power and efficiency of hydraulic and pneumatic components, and the hydraulic natural frequency of a valve-controlled actuator.
Plan trajectories and tune PD and PID position loops with feedforward, and estimate the limits set by friction, sampling and mechanical resonance.
Assess the reliability, electromagnetic compatibility and functional safety of a mechatronic design, and integrate its parts into a working system.

chapters.title: Mechatronic systems
chapters.summary: The elements of a mechatronic system, and the circuit basics needed to build one.

chapters.title: Sensors
chapters.summary: Measuring position, speed, acceleration, force, strain, pressure and temperature, and the specifications of sensors.

chapters.title: Signal conditioning and data acquisition
chapters.summary: Operational-amplifier circuits, bridges and filters, noise, analogue-to-digital conversion, sampling and aliasing.

chapters.title: Microcontrollers and embedded software
chapters.summary: Microcontroller architecture, digital input and output, timers, interrupts, pulse-width modulation and real-time programming.

chapters.title: Electric motors and drives
chapters.summary: DC, stepper and brushless motors, their models and torque–speed curves, and H-bridges and motor drives.

chapters.title: Hydraulic and pneumatic actuators
chapters.summary: Pumps, valves, cylinders and motors in fluid-power circuits, and their dynamics.

chapters.title: Motion control
chapters.summary: Closed-loop position and speed control of motor-driven axes, encoders, feedforward and trajectory following.

chapters.title: Designing mechatronic systems
chapters.summary: Integrating sensors, actuators and controllers, safety interlocks, and case studies from printers to vehicles.

history.title: Watt's centrifugal governor
history.detail: James Watt fits a flyweight governor to his rotative steam engines to regulate their speed — sensor, controller and actuator in one mechanism; James Clerk Maxwell analyses the stability of governors in 1868.

history.title: The hydraulic press
history.detail: Joseph Bramah patents the hydraulic press, applying Pascal's principle of the transmission of pressure to multiply force.

history.title: Electromagnetic rotation
history.detail: Michael Faraday demonstrates continuous rotation of a current-carrying wire around a magnet, the principle of the electric motor.

history.title: The bonded resistance strain gauge
history.detail: Arthur Ruge at MIT and Edward Simmons at Caltech independently develop the bonded wire strain gauge, the basis of load cells and pressure transducers; the patent is granted to Simmons in 1942.

history.title: Numerically controlled milling
history.detail: The MIT Servomechanisms Laboratory demonstrates a milling machine whose servo-driven axes follow coordinates read from punched tape, following a proposal by John T. Parsons.

history.title: The word mechatronics
history.detail: Tetsuro Mori, an engineer at Yaskawa Electric, coins the word mechatronics; Yaskawa registers it as a trademark in 1972 and later releases it for general use.

history.title: The microprocessor
history.detail: Intel's 4004 puts a CPU on one chip; Texas Instruments' single-chip TMS1000 microcontroller family, designed by Gary Boone and Michael Cochran, follows commercially in 1974.

history.title: Rate-monotonic scheduling
history.detail: C. L. Liu and James Layland publish the utilisation bound for scheduling periodic real-time tasks with fixed priorities, the basis of real-time operating systems.

history.title: Electronic anti-lock braking
history.detail: Bosch's electronic four-wheel anti-lock braking system enters series production on the Mercedes-Benz S-Class; Bosch presents the CAN bus in 1986.

history.title: VDI 2206
history.detail: The German engineering society VDI publishes guideline VDI 2206, a V-model design methodology for mechatronic systems (revised 2021).

references.title: Introduction to Mechatronics and Measurement Systems
references.note: 5th edition (McGraw-Hill). The standard undergraduate text: circuits, semiconductors, sensors, data acquisition, microcontrollers and actuators, with many worked examples.

references.title: Mechatronics: Electronic Control Systems in Mechanical and Electrical Engineering
references.note: 6th edition (Pearson). Broad, accessible coverage of sensors, signal conditioning, actuators, PLCs and system models.

references.title: Measurement Systems: Application and Design
references.note: 5th edition (McGraw-Hill). Thorough treatment of sensor principles and static and dynamic characteristics of measurement systems.

references.title: The Art of Electronics
references.note: 3rd edition (Cambridge University Press). The practical reference for op-amp circuits, filters, noise, converters, grounding and shielding.

references.title: Electric Motors and Drives: Fundamentals, Types and Applications
references.note: 5th edition (Newnes). Clear physical explanations of DC, stepper, induction and brushless motors and their drives.

references.title: Hydraulic Control Systems
references.note: Wiley. The classical analysis of valves, valve-controlled actuators and the hydraulic natural frequency; still the basis of hydraulic servo design.

references.title: Digital Control of Dynamic Systems
references.authors: G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell and M. L. Workman
references.note: 3rd edition (Addison-Wesley). Sampled-data control, sampling-rate selection, quantisation and the design of digital controllers, with a disk-drive servo case study.

references.title: Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering
references.note: Wiley. Grounding, shielding, cabling, decoupling and the control of emissions and susceptibility in electronic systems.
